title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
subtitle: ECDSA, ECDH, Ed25519, and why ECC beats RSA for size

whyItExists.problem: RSA requires large keys (2048+ bits) because factoring large integers, while hard, is not as hard as it could be. With better algorithms, RSA key sizes must keep growing to maintain security.
whyItExists.solution: ECC uses the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP), which is significantly harder than integer factorisation. A 256-bit ECC key provides the same security as a 3072-bit RSA key.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Digital signatures (ECDSA, Ed25519), key agreement (ECDH, X25519), TLS certificates. Use for all new asymmetric cryptography work.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Post-quantum environments (ECC is broken by Shor's algorithm, same as RSA).

explainModes.beginner: ECC does the same job as RSA but with much smaller keys. A 256-bit ECC key is as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key — that's 12x fewer bits for the same security.
explainModes.simple: ECC uses the mathematics of points on special curves. Adding two points on the curve is easy; finding which number you multiplied by to get a given point is extremely hard — that's the security.
explainModes.standard: ECC uses a group of points on an elliptic curve over a finite field. The private key is a scalar; the public key is the scalar multiplied by the base point. Security comes from the discrete logarithm being hard on elliptic curves.
explainModes.technical: ECDSA: sign with private key scalar d, verify with public key Q = d×G. ECDH: both parties derive shared secret from each other's public keys: Alice: d_A × Q_B; Bob: d_B × Q_A — these are equal because d_A × d_B × G = d_B × d_A × G. P-256 (NIST), secp256k1 (Bitcoin), Curve25519 (modern) are common curves.
explainModes.deepDive: Ed25519 (Edwards curve) is designed for constant-time operations — no timing side channels. ECDSA with P-256 requires a fresh random nonce per signature; nonce reuse (k-reuse) is catastrophic (Sony PlayStation 3 hack used this). Ed25519 is deterministic — no nonce needed. X25519 is the ECDH version of Curve25519.

content.text: ECC provides the same security as RSA with dramatically smaller keys. A 256-bit ECC key provides equivalent security to a 3072-bit RSA key. Smaller keys mean faster operations, less storage, and reduced bandwidth — critical for TLS certificates and mobile devices.

content.definition: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. Uses a private key to sign, public key to verify. Requires a unique random nonce per signature (nonce reuse breaks the system).
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman. A key agreement protocol. Two parties exchange public keys and independently compute the same shared secret without transmitting it.
A modern signing scheme based on Edwards Curve 25519. Deterministic (no random nonce per signature), constant-time, and significantly faster than ECDSA P-256.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
import os

# --- Generate ECDSA key pair (P-256 curve) ---
private_key = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
public_key = private_key.public_key()

# --- Sign ---
document = b"Git commit hash: abc123def456"
signature = private_key.sign(document, ec.ECDSA(hashes.SHA256()))
print("Signature length:", len(signature), "bytes")  # ~70 bytes (DER encoded)

# --- Verify ---
try:
    public_key.verify(signature, document, ec.ECDSA(hashes.SHA256()))
    print("ECDSA signature VALID")
except Exception:
    print("ECDSA signature INVALID")

# --- Export public key to PEM ---
pem = public_key.public_bytes(
    encoding=serialization.Encoding.PEM,
    format=serialization.PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo
)
print(pem.decode())

content.text: ECDSA requires a unique random nonce (k) for every signature. If you sign two different messages with the same k and the same private key, an attacker can recover your private key. This is how the PlayStation 3 was hacked in 2010. Prefer Ed25519 which is deterministic.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization

# --- Generate Ed25519 key pair ---
private_key = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
public_key = private_key.public_key()

# --- Sign (no hash parameter needed; Ed25519 handles it internally) ---
document = b"This is the message to sign"
signature = private_key.sign(document)
print("Ed25519 signature length:", len(signature), "bytes")  # always 64 bytes

# --- Verify ---
try:
    public_key.verify(signature, document)
    print("Ed25519 signature VALID")
except Exception:
    print("Ed25519 signature INVALID")

# --- Export for SSH / API ---
ssh_pub = public_key.public_bytes(
    encoding=serialization.Encoding.OpenSSH,
    format=serialization.PublicFormat.OpenSSH
)
print(ssh_pub.decode())  # ssh-ed25519 AAAA...

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
import os

# --- Alice and Bob each generate their own key pairs ---
alice_private = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
bob_private   = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())

alice_public = alice_private.public_key()
bob_public   = bob_private.public_key()

# --- Alice computes shared secret using Bob's public key ---
alice_shared = alice_private.exchange(ec.ECDH(), bob_public)

# --- Bob computes shared secret using Alice's public key ---
bob_shared = bob_private.exchange(ec.ECDH(), alice_public)

# They get the same 32 bytes WITHOUT transmitting the secret!
assert alice_shared == bob_shared
print("Shared secret established:", alice_shared.hex()[:16], "...")

# --- Derive AES key from shared secret using HKDF ---
aes_key = HKDF(
    algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
    length=32,
    salt=None,
    info=b"handshake session key"
).derive(alice_shared)
print("AES session key ready:", len(aes_key), "bytes")

a.name: ECDSA P-256
a.description: NIST curve, requires random nonce per signature
a.useWhen: TLS certificates, JWT ES256, FIPS compliance required

b.name: Ed25519
weaknesses: Not FIPS-approved (FIPS 186-5 adds it, but adoption lags)
b.useWhen: New systems — SSH, TLS client certs, Wireguard, modern JWTs

content.text: For new applications: use Ed25519 for signing and X25519 (Curve25519 ECDH) for key agreement. Both are constant-time, fast, and use the safest known curve parameters.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of ECC over RSA?
options: ECC is easier to implement from scratch
ECC provides equivalent security with much smaller key sizes
ECC is resistant to quantum computer attacks
questions.explanation: A 256-bit ECC key provides the same security as a 3072-bit RSA key. Smaller keys mean faster computation, less bandwidth, and simpler storage.

questions.question: Why is Ed25519 preferred over ECDSA P-256 for new systems?
options: Ed25519 produces longer signatures that are harder to fake
Ed25519 is deterministic — no random nonce needed per signature
questions.explanation: ECDSA requires a fresh random nonce per signature. If nonces are reused, the private key is recoverable. Ed25519 derives its nonce deterministically — this class of attack is impossible.

questions.question: What does ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) achieve?
options: It encrypts a message with the recipient's public key
It allows two parties to derive the same shared secret without transmitting it
It signs a document to prove authorship
It hashes a message to verify integrity
questions.explanation: ECDH is a key agreement protocol. Alice and Bob exchange public keys and each independently computes the same shared secret — which was never transmitted.

faq.a: An elliptic curve designed by Daniel Bernstein for high security and performance. Used in TLS 1.3, SSH, WireGuard, and Signal Protocol. The signing variant is Ed25519; the key agreement variant is X25519.

No. Shor's algorithm running on a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm, breaking ECC just as it breaks RSA. NIST's post-quantum standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) are the replacements.

faq.q: What is the difference between ECDH and ECDHE?
faq.a: ECDHE uses ephemeral keys — fresh key pairs generated for each connection. This provides forward secrecy: even if the server's long-term private key is later compromised, past sessions cannot be decrypted.

examples: GitHub requires Ed25519 or ECDSA for SSH keys; RSA-1024 is no longer accepted
TLS 1.3 uses X25519 or P-256 for key exchange in almost all HTTPS connections
The Sony PlayStation 3 (2010) ECDSA nonce-reuse vulnerability exposed the console's private key
